question: VOLMET is:

options.text: An automatic report of the weather seen by the aircraft's own weather radar, sent to ATC
A broadcast for aircraft in flight of reports and forecasts for a group of aerodromes
A warning issued only for volcanic ash clouds affecting air routes
A recorded broadcast for a single aerodrome, including the runway in use

explanation: The name comes from the French "vol" (flight) and "météo". VOLMET gives METARs, TRENDs, and sometimes TAFs and SIGMETs, for several aerodromes in turn.

question: VOLMET broadcasts are made on:

options.text: HF only, so it can be received anywhere in the world
The ILS localiser frequency of each aerodrome covered
VHF only, so it can only be received within line of sight of the station
VHF for regional services, and HF for long-range ones such as oceanic

explanation: HF VOLMETs, such as Shannon VOLMET for the North Atlantic, allow information to be received far from the transmitter.

question: VOLMET broadcasts are typically updated:

options.text: Only when severe weather is expected
Every 6 hours, with the synoptic charts
Every half hour, as new reports arrive
Once a day, before the first departures

explanation: Updates follow the routine METAR cycle.

question: A disadvantage of VOLMET compared with requesting information from ATC is that:

options.text: Several aerodromes are broadcast in turn, so the pilot may wait for the one needed
It is always in coded form, which must be decoded before any of it can be used
It never includes the visibility, which must be requested from ATC
It only covers aerodromes behind the aircraft, not those ahead

explanation: The broadcast cycles through its list of aerodromes, so it can take a few minutes for the wanted aerodrome to come around.

question: VOLMET information is broadcast:

options.text: In Morse code only, on the HF frequencies
In plain language, from METARs with TREND, sometimes with TAFs and SIGMETs
As a graphical chart sent to the cockpit display
In METAR code only, read out letter by letter on the frequency for each station

explanation: Spoken plain language makes it easy to understand in flight.

question: In flight, VOLMET is most useful to the pilot for:

options.text: Obtaining the take-off clearance and departure instructions from ATC before take-off
Finding the position of jet streams along the route
Checking the aircraft's fuel state against the flight plan
Checking the weather at destination and alternates, and deciding whether to divert

explanation: Planning ahead with VOLMET frequencies lets the crew monitor conditions at destination and alternates during the flight.

question: The HF VOLMET of particular importance for North Atlantic flights is broadcast from:

options.text: Shannon
London Heathrow
Rome
Frankfurt

explanation: Shannon VOLMET covers many European and North Atlantic aerodromes on HF frequencies.

question: ATIS is:

options.text: An automatic warning of windshear given on the approach
A broadcast of the weather at many aerodromes in sequence, one after another
A continuous broadcast of current aerodrome and weather information
A satellite weather service received by data link

explanation: ATIS reduces congestion on busy ATC frequencies by giving routine information on a separate channel.

question: Each ATIS broadcast is identified by:

options.text: The time at which the next routine METAR is due to be issued
The designator of the runway in use
A phonetic alphabet letter that changes with each update
The elevation of the aerodrome

explanation: For example, Information Bravo replaces Information Alpha after an update.

question: On first contact with ATC, a pilot should:

options.text: State the identifying letter of the latest ATIS received
Ask the controller to read out the ATIS again
Read back the whole of the ATIS message to the controller
Give the QNH from the ATIS, without the letter

explanation: The letter tells the controller the pilot has the current information, allowing the controller to omit those details.

question: In an ATIS broadcast, the surface wind is given:

options.text: As a variable direction only
In degrees magnetic, in knots
In degrees true, in metres per second
In degrees true, in knots

explanation: Winds passed for take-off and landing, including ATIS, are magnetic so they relate directly to runway headings.

question: An ATIS broadcast would typically include:

options.text: The TAFs for all the alternate aerodromes in the region
The upper winds and temperatures at FL300 and above over the aerodrome and its approaches
The positions and core levels of jet streams near the aerodrome
Runway, wind, visibility, weather, cloud, temperature, dew point, QNH and warnings

explanation: It may also include the transition level, expected approach type and runway surface conditions.

question: An ATIS is updated:

options.text: Whenever a significant change occurs, with a new code letter
Only once every 24 hours, at the start of the day's operations
Only when a pilot asks for an update
Only at 0000 and 1200 UTC each day

explanation: Any significant change prompts a new ATIS and a new letter.

question: At some aerodromes, ATIS is broadcast:

options.text: Only by data link to the cockpit printer
On a VOR voice channel, or separately for arrivals and departures
Only on HF, so that it can be received at long range from the aerodrome
On the ILS glidepath frequency for the main runway

explanation: Using a VOR voice channel frees VHF communication frequencies. Busy aerodromes may have separate arrival and departure ATIS.

question: If a pilot does not acknowledge receipt of the latest ATIS, the controller will:

options.text: Refuse to provide any service until it is received
Instruct the pilot to divert to an alternate
Pass the essential aerodrome information to the pilot
Assume the pilot has it anyway and continue

explanation: The controller must ensure the pilot has the necessary information.

question: Even when the pilot reports having the current ATIS, the controller normally still confirms:

options.text: The ATIS letter
The cloud type
The dew point
The QNH

explanation: The altimeter setting is critical for safety, so it is usually confirmed.

question: A special air-report should be made by a pilot who encounters:

options.text: Severe turbulence or icing, severe mountain waves, thunderstorms or volcanic ash
An outside air temperature about 2°C above the forecast
Light turbulence in fair-weather cumulus, just below the cloud base on a summer afternoon
A clear sky at cruise level with good visibility

explanation: Special air-reports warn other aircraft and the meteorological service of hazards, and may lead to a SIGMET.

question: Reports of turbulence or icing from pilots are especially valuable because:

options.text: They are used by ATC to calculate the QNH for each region
They are required from every flight, even in clear weather
They replace the need for routine METARs at all of the aerodromes along the route
They are hard to observe from the ground, and reports confirm or correct forecasts

explanation: Forecasters rely on air-reports for information such as cloud tops, icing and turbulence that ground instruments cannot measure.

question: Routine automated reports from aircraft (for example via data link) mainly provide:

options.text: The cloud base at each aerodrome passed
Wind and temperature data along the route
The visibility at destination aerodromes
Runway friction measurements at destination

explanation: Automated air-reports greatly increase the number of upper-air observations, especially over oceans.

question: A pilot who encounters severe icing not mentioned in the forecast should:

options.text: Report it only after landing, in the technical log
Say nothing unless the controller asks about it later in the flight
Report it to ATC promptly, with position, level, time, intensity and type
Report it only if the aircraft has de-icing equipment

explanation: Prompt reporting allows other pilots to be warned and may result in a SIGMET.

question: During pre-flight planning, a pilot should note:

options.text: Only the HF frequencies listed for the departure aerodrome
No frequencies, as ATC will always pass the weather
VOLMET and ATIS frequencies for destination, alternates and en-route aerodromes
Only the ATIS frequency of the departure aerodrome, as the others are not needed

explanation: Having frequencies ready allows quick in-flight updates, particularly if a diversion becomes necessary.

question: Which source gives the most up-to-date weather for a specific aerodrome as an aircraft begins its approach?

options.text: A TAF for the aerodrome issued 6 hours earlier
A SIGWX chart valid at the time of arrival
A climatological summary for the month
The aerodrome's ATIS, or information passed by ATC

explanation: ATIS carries the latest observation and is updated whenever conditions change.

question: When reviewing METARs in flight, it is useful to check aerodromes upwind of the destination because:

options.text: They are always closer to the aircraft than the destination
They show weather that may soon arrive at the destination
They report the destination's RVR
Their QNH is always the same as at the destination

explanation: Weather moves with the wind, so upwind stations give an early warning of approaching changes.

question: Which statement about the information in VOLMET and ATIS is correct?

options.text: ATIS covers one aerodrome with operational details; VOLMET gives weather for several
Both are available only on HF, for oceanic flights
Neither includes the QNH, which must be requested
VOLMET gives the runway in use; ATIS gives the weather at many aerodromes in turn

explanation: ATIS combines weather with aerodrome operational information; VOLMET is purely meteorological, for several aerodromes.

question: In-flight weather updates may also be obtained by data link, for example:

options.text: Only from the aircraft's own weather radar
D-ATIS and METAR/TAF requests through the aircraft's data link
Only by listening to the scheduled HF VOLMET broadcasts on the hour
Only after landing, from the briefing office

explanation: Data link services deliver text weather directly to the cockpit, avoiding frequency congestion.

question: A METAR received in flight shows the destination visibility well below minimums, with a TREND of NOSIG. The pilot should expect:

options.text: No significant improvement within two hours, so a diversion should be planned
That NOSIG cancels the visibility given in the report
A rapid improvement in visibility at destination within the next 30 minutes
That the visibility will only be forecast in the next TAF

explanation: NOSIG means no significant change is expected in the next two hours.

question: An HF VOLMET broadcast is scheduled at fixed times each hour, for example at 00 and 30 minutes past. This means:

options.text: It can only be received by aircraft on the ground
The broadcast is continuous, so it can be heard at any time of the hour
The pilot must listen at the right times to hear the aerodromes needed
It is only available during an emergency

explanation: HF VOLMET stations share frequencies and transmit in allocated time slots.

question: The ATIS gives the transition level. This is useful to a pilot on descent because it tells them:

options.text: The height of the cloud base
When to call the tower frequency
When to switch on the landing lights on the approach
When to change from the standard setting to the QNH

explanation: On descent, the altimeter is set to QNH on passing the transition level.

question: An arriving pilot hears an ATIS reporting "windshear reported on final approach runway 27". The pilot should:

options.text: Ignore it, as ATIS only gives routine weather and never includes warnings
Land on runway 09 instead, without asking for permission
Expect speed and flight path changes; consider extra margins or delaying
Disconnect the autopilot immediately, whatever the approach

explanation: Windshear reports warn of hazards on the approach path. Operators' procedures describe how to respond.

question: Which in-flight information source is best for obtaining weather at several aerodromes along a long oceanic route?

options.text: HF VOLMET or data link services
The departure ATIS
A ground-based weather radar
The destination's VHF ATIS while still 2000 nm away

explanation: HF has long range, and data link can provide text weather anywhere within coverage.
